bibliography.title: Densely Connected Stacked U-network for Filament Segmentation in Microscopy Images

review_notes: A second pass checked methods, figures, tables, results, available appendices or supplements, and limitations against the local PDF.
The local publisher PDF contains no appended supplement.
Independent human review remains outstanding.

summary.text: The method stacks three modified U-Net modules, adds cross-connections at matching feature-map sizes, and applies weighted intermediate supervision to segmentation outputs.

details.text: Each of the three modules has two max-pooling and two up-sampling steps, with shared 1x1 output convolution and cross-connections between matching feature-map sizes.

losses.value: Dice coefficient loss on three module outputs with weights 0.2, 0.3, and 0.5

data.value: 25 full-resolution training images and 28 test images
SOAX weak masks, a single-module U-Net trained on 709,800 patches, and manual expert correction

validation_design.text: The reported experiments use 25 full-resolution microtubule images for training and 28 for testing; the microtubule-trained network is also applied to an actin dataset.

reported_results.text: On the microtubule test set, the cross-connected network at 15 epochs reports IoU 0.9439 and SKIoU 0.9775; the no-cross-connection variant has the highest listed SKIoU at 0.9792.
On the actin dataset, the microtubule-trained cross-connected network reports IoU 0.9140 and SKIoU 0.9580, with smaller gaps than the compared U-Net qualitatively.

claimed_contributions.text: The authors present a densely connected stacked U-network and a semi-automatic annotation strategy for microscopy filaments.

author_stated_limitations.text: The authors warn that IoU may be biased because the test annotations were manually corrected from U-Net outputs.

other_reported_findings.text: The authors report fewer disconnected microtubules and fragments than a single U-Net, while noting that the numerical SKIoU scores of the neural networks are close.

main_strength.text: This is the corpus's closest primary evidence for a 2D microscopy-filament semantic-segmentation baseline with a documented annotation workflow.

main_limitation.text: The study evaluates confocal semantic masks rather than direct STED data or explicit instances, and its IoU evaluation may inherit annotation-model bias.

best_use_case.text: Baseline mask segmentation and semi-automatic label bootstrapping for microscopy fibers.

transfer_to_sted.rationale: The task and structures are close to the project, but STED-specific noise, resolution, and topology recovery are not evaluated.
assumptions: 2D STED fibers can be represented by patches similar to the confocal inputs.
risks: Semantic masks may remain disconnected or merge crossings despite improved continuity.

evidence_spans.text: The paper addresses filament segmentation in confocal microscopy images and introduces a deep network intended to reduce falsely disconnected filaments.
evidence_spans.notes: Publisher PDF.

evidence_spans.text: Experts corrected 53 full-resolution segmentations; 25 images were used for training and 28 for testing, and a separate 10-image actin dataset was created.
evidence_spans.notes: The preceding page describes SOAX and U-Net-assisted annotation.

evidence_spans.text: Three U-Net-like modules are stacked; each produces a segmentation map, weighted intermediate losses are used, and matching feature-map sizes receive cross-connections.
evidence_spans.notes: Architecture continues onto PDF page 6.

evidence_spans.text: The annotation single-module model is trained for 20 epochs with batch size 64; the final proposed segmentation network is trained for 15 epochs with batch size 64 on 5,032,407 128x128 patches. All networks use Adam at 0.0001, Dice loss, and dropout 0.2.
evidence_spans.notes: The 20-epoch annotation model and 15-epoch final segmentation model are distinct.

evidence_spans.text: Evaluation uses IoU and Skeletonized IoU; the authors explicitly warn that IoU may be biased because test annotations were manually corrected from U-Net outputs.
evidence_spans.notes: SKIoU is explicitly defined in Equation 1.

evidence_spans.text: The 15-epoch cross-connected model reports IoU 0.9439 and SKIoU 0.9775; the no-cross model reports SKIoU 0.9792, and the discussion says numerical SKIoUs are close.
evidence_spans.notes: The qualitative continuity claim is author-reported.

evidence_spans.text: The microtubule-trained proposed network reports actin IoU 0.9140 and SKIoU 0.9580; the authors describe fewer fragments and gaps than U-Net.
evidence_spans.notes: No actin-specific training is reported.

evidence_spans.text: The authors claim contributions of a densely connected stacked U-network and a semi-automatic annotation strategy.
evidence_spans.notes: Future quantification and tracking are described as future work, not achieved results.

evidence_spans.text: SOAX creates weak masks from 24 maximum-intensity projections of 17-slice stacks; augmentation yields 709,800 patches used to train a single-module U-Net before expert correction of a larger image set.
evidence_spans.notes: This evidence concerns the annotation model, not the final stacked segmentation model.

bibliography.title: clDice - a Novel Topology-Preserving Loss Function for Tubular Structure Segmentation

review_notes: A second pass checked methods, figures, tables, results, available appendices or supplements, and limitations against the local PDF.
The local source is arXiv v7 dated 2022; publication metadata refers to the 2021 CVPR paper.
Independent human review remains outstanding.

domain.raw_value: tubular and curvilinear structure segmentation across vessels, roads, and neurons

imaging_modalities.raw_value: retinal images, road imagery, neuron data, synthetic vessels, and volumetric brain-vessel scans

summary.text: clDice measures centerline overlap between prediction and label, while soft-clDice uses differentiable iterative soft-skeletonization so the measure can be included in a training objective.

family.raw_value: backbone-agnostic loss evaluated with U-Net and FCN architectures

details.text: The experiments use 2D and 3D U-Net and FCN models while holding architecture fixed across loss comparisons.

inputs.value: 2D images and 3D volumes with binary segmentation labels

training.value: 5 to 25, selected to match the largest observed tubular radius

value: DRIVE: 30 images in three-fold cross-validation, 10 test
Massachusetts Roads: 120 images in three-fold cross-validation, 13 test
CREMI: 324 images in three-fold cross-validation, 51 test

postprocessing.value: iterative soft-skeletonization used inside the loss

validation_design.text: The loss is compared with soft-Dice on 2D and 3D U-Net and FCN architectures across five datasets. The appendix gives dataset-specific cross-validation or train/validation/test splits and reports the model with the highest validation clDice.

reported_results.text: The main experiments report aggregate improvements from adding soft-clDice, but supplementary synthetic-vessel results show that individual Dice or clDice values do not improve for every nonzero alpha and loss pairing.
For batch size 4 and 1024x1024 images on an RTX-8000, the reported training-time overhead is 1.35 seconds versus 1.24 seconds for soft-Dice.

claimed_contributions.text: The paper introduces clDice as a topology-oriented similarity measure and soft-clDice as a differentiable loss component for arbitrary segmentation networks.

author_stated_limitations.text: The authors state that improved differentiable skeletonization and multiclass theoretical and experimental studies remain future work.

other_reported_findings.text: The topology guarantee is stated under assumptions including foreground and background structures that are homotopy-equivalent to topological graphs.
The supplementary sweep states that improvement holds for almost, not all, nonzero alpha values; alpha is dataset- and objective-specific.

main_strength.text: The contribution can be evaluated independently of the segmentation backbone and directly targets connectivity-sensitive behavior.

main_limitation.text: No STED cytoskeletal dataset is evaluated, and the guarantee has mathematical assumptions that may not cover noisy multiclass or instance-level fiber images.

best_use_case.text: A connectivity-aware auxiliary objective for a binary fiber-mask baseline, evaluated alongside region overlap.

transfer_to_sted.rationale: The objective is backbone-agnostic and tested on thin connected structures, but STED-specific data and instance continuity are absent.
assumptions: Binary STED labels have meaningful centerlines and compatible topology.
risks: Soft-skeleton iterations and alpha require dataset-specific tuning.
Connectivity of a semantic mask does not resolve filament identity at crossings.

evidence_spans.text: The paper introduces clDice and soft-clDice for topology-aware segmentation and evaluates connected structures in 2D and 3D.
evidence_spans.notes: Local PDF is the later arXiv version.

evidence_spans.locator: Definition of topology precision, topology sensitivity, and clDice
evidence_spans.text: clDice is the harmonic mean of topology precision and topology sensitivity computed from mask-skeleton intersections; the guarantee is developed under stated topological assumptions.
evidence_spans.notes: The exact theorem conditions extend across subsequent pages.

evidence_spans.text: Iterative soft-skeletonization uses 5 to 25 iterations in the experiments, and the combined objective weights soft-Dice and soft-clDice with alpha between 0 and 0.5.
evidence_spans.notes: Iteration count is linked to the largest observed tubular radius.

evidence_spans.text: Main experiments use 2D and 3D U-Net and FCN models on five datasets, sweep alpha from 0.1 to 0.5, and report aggregate improvements across volumetric, graph, and topology measures.
evidence_spans.notes: This aggregate statement does not imply that every metric improves at every alpha.

evidence_spans.text: Table 1 compares Dice, accuracy, clDice, Betti errors, street-mover distance, Euler-characteristic error, and junction F1 across datasets and losses.
evidence_spans.notes: Individual numerical values are not reproduced in the card.

evidence_spans.text: The reported 1024x1024 training times are 1.35 seconds for soft-clDice and 1.24 seconds for soft-Dice; improved differentiable skeletonization and multiclass studies are left for future work.
evidence_spans.notes: Inference time is unchanged for identical architectures.

evidence_spans.text: The appendix reports the exact DRIVE, Roads, CREMI, synthetic-3D, and Vessap splits and selects the model with the highest validation clDice.
evidence_spans.notes: Split counts were checked individually against the appendix.

evidence_spans.locator: Table caption and synthetic-vessel alpha sweep
evidence_spans.text: Supplementary experiments sweep alpha from 0.001 to 0.5 with BCE, soft-Dice, and MSE baselines; the table includes nonzero-alpha settings where individual Dice or clDice values do not exceed the corresponding baseline.
evidence_spans.notes: The caption says improvement holds for almost alpha greater than zero, preserving the reported qualification.

bibliography.title: DeepVesselNet: Vessel Segmentation, Centerline Prediction, and Bifurcation Detection in 3-D Angiographic Volumes

review_notes: A second pass checked methods, figures, tables, results, available appendices or supplements, and limitations against the local PDF.
The local journal PDF contains no appended supplementary section.
Independent human review remains outstanding.

imaging_modalities.raw_value: TOF MRA, micro-CT angiography, and synthetic angiographic volumes

summary.text: DeepVesselNet uses sparse cross-hair filters, an extreme class-balancing objective, synthetic vascular-tree pretraining, and separate binary networks for vessel, centerline, and bifurcation targets.

family.raw_value: five-layer fully convolutional DeepVesselNet-FCN with cross-hair filters

details.text: The preferred FCN has five layers, no down-sampling or up-sampling, accepts arbitrary-size volumes at inference, and outputs a same-size map.

losses.value: L1 extreme class balancing plus L2 false-prediction-rate correction

data.value: 136 simulated 325x304x600 volumes; 20 held out for testing
40 TOF-MRA volumes with fully and partially annotated subsets used for validation, testing, and finetuning

validation_design.text: Architectural variants are pretrained on synthetic volumes, evaluated on held-out synthetic data, and finetuned or evaluated on clinical angiography; annotated clinical centerline and bifurcation targets are unavailable.

reported_results.text: Synthetic pretraining followed by clinical finetuning reports Dice 86.68% versus 86.39% from scratch and convergence in 1200 versus 1800 iterations; the authors state that the accuracy difference is small.

The centerline results attribute poorer performance of subsampling architectures to loss of fine details, and DeepVesselNet-FCN reports bifurcation precision 78.80 and recall 92.97 on the stated evaluation.

claimed_contributions.text: The authors present cross-hair filters, stable extreme class balancing, and synthetic transfer learning for 3D vessel segmentation and structural targets.

author_stated_limitations.text: The paper leaves a unified multiclass or hierarchical model for simultaneous vessel, centerline, and bifurcation prediction as future work.

other_reported_findings.text: The authors report that subsampling can reduce performance for voxel-sized structures and that synthetic pretraining mainly reduces convergence time in the clinical segmentation experiment.
Figure 10 reports better bifurcation detections in smaller than larger vessels and shows dense intersections being predicted as one large bifurcation.

main_strength.text: The paper provides explicit 3D structural targets and a documented strategy for synthetic pretraining under severe class imbalance.

main_limitation.text: The evidence is from angiographic vessels, with separate binary networks and no direct microscopy or STED experiment.

best_use_case.text: Adjacent-domain evidence for auxiliary centerline or junction-related supervision and synthetic pretraining.

transfer_to_sted.rationale: Structural concepts are relevant, but 3D angiography, vessel-specific bifurcations, and separate networks differ materially from the intended STED setting.
assumptions: Fiber centerlines can be labelled or derived reliably.
risks: Vessel bifurcation semantics may not match crossings or branches in cytoskeletal networks.
The no-subsampling architecture may be unnecessarily costly for 2D data.

comparison_summary.task_focus: 3D vessel mask, centerline, and bifurcation prediction

evidence_spans.text: DeepVesselNet addresses 3D vessel segmentation, centerline prediction, and bifurcation detection in angiographic volumes.
evidence_spans.notes: Final journal article dated December 2020.

evidence_spans.text: The method combines a stable class-balancing term with false-prediction-rate correction and introduces a synthetic vascular-tree generator for transfer learning.
evidence_spans.notes: The loss is designed for very small foreground fractions.

evidence_spans.text: The paper reports 136 synthetic volumes with vessel, centerline, and bifurcation labels and describes 40 clinical TOF-MRA volumes divided among annotated subsets.
evidence_spans.notes: Twenty synthetic volumes are held out for testing.

evidence_spans.text: The FCN is a five-layer fully convolutional architecture without down/up-sampling and can process full volumes at test time.
evidence_spans.notes: Alternative VNet and U-Net variants are also evaluated.

evidence_spans.text: Training uses 64x64x64 boxes, unregularized SGD, learning rate 0.01 for pretraining and 0.001 for finetuning, each decayed by 0.99 every 200 iterations.
evidence_spans.notes: Full volumes can be used after kernels are trained.

evidence_spans.text: With pretraining, the reported clinical Dice is 86.68% and convergence takes 1200 iterations; without pretraining, Dice is 86.39% and convergence takes 1800 iterations.
evidence_spans.notes: The authors state accuracy differs little while convergence improves.

evidence_spans.text: Subsampling models lose fine centerline details; DeepVesselNet-FCN reports bifurcation precision 78.80 and recall 92.97. Figure 10 shows poorer detections in larger vessels and merged predictions at dense intersections.
evidence_spans.notes: Bifurcation evaluation uses 5x5x5 neighborhoods.

evidence_spans.text: The authors identify subsampling risk for voxel-sized structures and propose future unified multiclass or hierarchical prediction of the three targets.
evidence_spans.notes: The current implementation uses three separate binary networks.

bibliography.title: Quantifying Actin Filaments in Microscopic Images Using Keypoint Detection Techniques and a Fast Marching Algorithm

review_notes: A second pass checked methods, figures, tables, results, available appendices or supplements, and limitations against the local PDF.
The paper mentions additional qualitative supplemental results, but no supplemental file is appended to the local PDF.
Independent human review remains outstanding.

domain.raw_value: actin filament quantification in microscopic images

task_levels.raw_value: filament count and length estimation using fast marching

summary.text: A pretrained filament segmenter produces a binary mask, a modified ResNet-101 predicts junction and endpoint heatmaps plus offsets, Hough voting refines keypoints, and fast marching estimates filament counts and lengths.

family.raw_value: pretrained filament segmenter followed by modified ResNet-101 keypoint detector

details.text: The detector predicts heatmaps and two-channel offsets for junctions and endpoints, followed by Hough voting and local-maximum selection.

inputs.value: binary segmentation from the pretrained network

losses.value: Dice coefficient loss and L1 loss penalize heatmap and offset prediction errors; the paper does not explicitly assign one loss to each output

data.value: 10 images of size 1740x840 generated as maximum-intensity projections from 17 slices
10,000 images of size 128x128 with up to six one-pixel curves, junction labels, and dilation kernels from 3 to 7

postprocessing.value: Hough voting, maximum filtering, and thresholded local maxima
fast marching from junctions and endpoints; doubled local distance-map peaks estimate filament lengths

metrics.value: percentage difference in total length, count, and average length; manual count on two selected images

validation_design.text: The method is compared with SOAX and a skeletonization-based approach on ten images; only two selected images receive manual filament counts.

reported_results.text: The authors report similar total lengths among methods, counts closer to manual counts on two selected images, more precise junction localization than skeletonization qualitatively, and seconds per image versus hours for SOAX.

claimed_contributions.text: The paper adapts keypoint detection to filament junctions and combines segmentation, keypoints, and fast marching for actin length and count estimation.

author_stated_limitations.text: The authors state that the method does not obtain orientation angles or curvatures.

other_reported_findings.text: The paper argues that naive skeletonization can split a junction into multiple points and create false short segments.
Manual filament counts are reported for only two selected images, so the claimed count advantage is not established over the full ten-image set.

main_strength.text: The pipeline directly connects structural keypoints to count and length outputs instead of stopping at a semantic mask.

main_limitation.text: Validation is small and lacks full instance-level ground truth; keypoint training hyperparameters are not reported in the paper.

best_use_case.text: Evidence for endpoint and junction targets when the desired outputs are filament counts and lengths.

transfer_to_sted.rationale: The biological object and output statistics are relevant, but the small evaluation and synthetic keypoint labels limit confidence.
assumptions: STED masks permit stable junction and endpoint definitions.
risks: Errors from segmentation and keypoint detection propagate into fast marching.
Dense crossings may not correspond to true biological junctions.

comparison_summary.task_focus: actin segmentation, keypoint detection, and quantification
comparison_summary.main_transfer_risk: small evaluation without full instance ground truth

checked_locations: PDF pages 3-5, Methods Sections 2-4 and Analysis and Results

evidence_spans.text: The paper combines binary segmentation, modified ResNet detection of junctions and endpoints, and fast marching to estimate actin filament number and length.
evidence_spans.notes: Final publication metadata appears at the top of the manuscript.

evidence_spans.text: The real set has ten 1740x840 maximum-intensity projections from 17 slices; synthetic keypoint training uses 10,000 128x128 images with up to six curves and random dilation.
evidence_spans.notes: The PDF viewer page is used because manuscript pagination is not publication pagination.

evidence_spans.text: A pretrained segmenter supplies the binary input; ResNet-101 predicts keypoint heatmaps and offsets, Hough voting refines them, and the paper uses Dice and L1 losses for heatmap and offset errors without explicitly mapping each loss to one output.
evidence_spans.notes: Optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and epoch count are not reported; loss-to-output assignment is ambiguous.

evidence_spans.section: 3.4 Quantification analysis using a fast marching algorithm
evidence_spans.text: Fast marching starts from predicted junctions and endpoints; doubled local maxima of the geodesic distance map estimate path lengths and the number of peaks estimates filament count.
evidence_spans.notes: The method treats paths between keypoints as filaments.

evidence_spans.text: Ten images are compared with SOAX and skeletonization, but manual counts are provided for only two selected images; the authors report closer counts on those images and seconds per image versus hours for SOAX.
evidence_spans.notes: The limited manual-count selection restricts generalization.

evidence_spans.text: The authors identify inability to obtain orientation angle and curvature as the main limitation.
evidence_spans.notes: Explicit author-stated limitation.

bibliography.title: Intersection to Overpass: Instance Segmentation on Filamentous Structures With an Orientation-Aware Neural Network and Terminus Pairing Algorithm

review_notes: A second pass checked methods, figures, tables, results, available appendices or supplements, and limitations against the local PDF.
The author-manuscript PDF places Tables 1 and 2 on PDF pages 23 and 24.
Independent human review remains outstanding.

imaging_modalities.raw_value: microscopy images of microtubules plus a road-network transfer set

summary.text: Six parallel U-Net-like hourglass branches predict orientation-associated skeleton layers; a merged reconstruction and overlap loss constrain them, and a terminus-pairing algorithm reconnects fragments into instances.

family.raw_value: six parallel orientation-associated hourglass modules adapted from U-Net

details.text: The branches cover six 30-degree orientation intervals from 0 to 180 degrees, and their outputs are merged to reconstruct the input while pairwise overlap is discouraged.

inputs.value: 64x64 dilated binary filament patches for training; full segmentation results for inference

losses.value: revised Dice overlap penalty with weight 0.01

data.value: 120,000 64x64x7 targets assembled from 180,000 generated curves distributed across six orientation buckets
a ten-image instance-labelled dataset plus a seven-image public microtubule dataset

postprocessing.value: recursive local search across layers using overlap, propagation-direction similarity, endpoint-vector similarity, and distance thresholds

validation_design.text: The network is evaluated on an author-created ten-image microtubule set, a public seven-image microtubule set, and qualitatively on a road dataset.

reported_results.text: On the in-house dataset, Table 1 reports F1 0.7161, precision 0.6456, recall 0.8189, and average SKIoU 0.8166 for the proposed method; the authors warn that manual correction from their outputs may bias results.

On the seven-image public dataset, total filament count is 196 versus manual 191.8±3.6 and Zeder's 200; the authors explicitly state that the closer total does not establish that their method outperforms Zeder's, and they document reconnection failures.
Reported per-image runtimes are about six hours for SOAX, four minutes for SIFNE, and thirty minutes for the proposed method.

claimed_contributions.text: The paper reformulates filament instance segmentation as orientation-associated fragment prediction followed by terminus pairing.

author_stated_limitations.text: Merged side outputs can leave gaps, terminus pairing can choose a geometrically plausible but wrong candidate, and inaccurate input segmentation causes failure.

other_reported_findings.text: The authors found empirically that six orientation intervals balance angular resolution against over-fragmentation.
The proposed method is reported as faster than SOAX but slower than SIFNE, and a closer public-dataset count is not claimed as proof of superior extraction.

main_strength.text: This paper addresses filament identity at crossings rather than only improving foreground connectivity.

main_limitation.text: The discrete orientation representation and heuristic pairing introduce failure modes and depend on an accurate upstream segmentation.

best_use_case.text: A targeted option when crossing-specific instance continuity is a measured dominant error.

transfer_to_sted.rationale: The microscopy task and crossing problem are relevant, but synthetic training, discrete orientations, and biased in-house labels reduce certainty.
assumptions: Filament direction is locally stable within the chosen bins.
risks: Curved or kinked fibers split across bins.
Nearby termini can be paired incorrectly.

comparison_summary.main_transfer_risk: orientation bins and heuristic pairing can fail

evidence_spans.text: The method uses six orientation-associated branches and terminus pairing to extract individual filaments at intersections.
evidence_spans.notes: The final edited citation identifies the 2019 CVPR Workshops publication.

evidence_spans.text: Six parallel hourglass branches cover consecutive 30-degree bins, produce orientation layers, merge to a skeleton reconstruction, and are constrained to minimize overlap.
evidence_spans.notes: Each branch is U-Net-like.

evidence_spans.text: Training uses 120,000 64x64 patches assembled from orientation-bucketed synthetic curves, five epochs, batch size 64, Adam at 0.0001, and overlap-loss weight 0.01.
evidence_spans.notes: The source also describes 180,000 generated strand images before sample assembly.

evidence_spans.text: Fragments are recursively paired using overlap cases first, then propagation direction, inter-terminus vector similarity, and distance thresholds.
evidence_spans.notes: The pairing is heuristic and threshold-based.

evidence_spans.locator: Evaluation protocol and in-house dataset discussion
evidence_spans.text: Evaluation uses SKIoU-based instance matching and precision, recall, and F-measure on ten microscopy images; the authors warn that manual correction from their outputs may bias results.
evidence_spans.notes: Bias warning is explicit.

evidence_spans.text: The public set contains seven 5000x5000 images and about 192 manually counted filaments; failures are shown, and runtimes are reported as about six hours for SOAX, four minutes for SIFNE, and thirty minutes for the proposed method.
evidence_spans.notes: Road data lack instance labels.

evidence_spans.text: The authors list incomplete merged reconstruction, wrong terminus pairing, and sensitivity to inaccurate upstream segmentation as limitations.
evidence_spans.notes: Explicit author-stated limitations.

evidence_spans.text: The pipeline diagram identifies a segmentation result as the input to orientation-layer prediction and terminus pairing.
evidence_spans.notes: This establishes that the method consumes an upstream binary segmentation rather than raw microscopy intensity.

evidence_spans.text: For the proposed method, Table 1 reports F1 0.7161, precision 0.6456, recall 0.8189, and average SKIoU 0.8166.
evidence_spans.notes: The table is on PDF page 23, not the narrative evaluation page.

evidence_spans.text: Across seven images, Table 2 reports total manual count 191.8±3.6, Zeder's method 200, and the proposed method 196.
evidence_spans.notes: The narrative explicitly cautions that the closer total does not prove outperformance.

bibliography.title: SOAX: A software for quantification of 3D biopolymer networks

review_notes: A second pass checked methods, figures, tables, results, available appendices or supplements, and limitations against the local PDF.
The local publisher PDF and its discussion/methods pages were checked; no separate supplement is appended.
Independent human review remains outstanding.

imaging_modalities.raw_value: confocal fluorescence microscopy of actin bundles, microtubules, and fission-yeast actin cables

summary.text: SOAX initializes short active contours on intensity ridges, evolves and stretches them along filament centerlines, merges contacts, reconfigures junctions, and exposes manual editing and quantitative analysis.

details.text: The extraction stages are SOAC initialization, sequential evolution and merging, and junction configuration by cutting and splicing local contours.

outputs.raw_value: network topology represented by configured contours and junctions

data.value: synthetic noisy 3D networks plus confocal actin-bundle, microtubule, and fission-yeast actin-cable examples

postprocessing.value: cluster nearby T-junctions, then cut and splice contours to avoid sharp ends or bends
cut, extend, modify, or delete contours and junctions

metrics.value: F-function based on local signal-to-noise behavior of extracted contours

validation_design.text: Synthetic networks with known ground truth evaluate extraction accuracy and parameter selection; experimental confocal datasets demonstrate 3D biological-network analysis.

reported_results.text: On synthetic data, the F-function yields a small candidate set with behavior similar to ground-truth Hausdorff and vertex-error optima, but a user still selects among candidates and low-SNR cases are more sensitive.

claimed_contributions.text: SOAX provides open-source centerline and junction extraction, visualization, manual editing, quantitative analysis, and a parameter-evaluation procedure.

author_stated_limitations.text: Parameters depend on biopolymer type and image SNR; low-SNR cases require guided manual candidate selection, wide-field background may require deconvolution, and anisotropic z resolution can create false z-aligned contours.

other_reported_findings.text: Large ridge thresholds miss dim filaments, low thresholds initialize contours on noise, large stretch factors overshoot tips, and small stretch factors stop early.
The F-function narrows parameter candidates but does not remove user selection; the authors state that guided fine-tuning is especially necessary at low SNR.

main_strength.text: SOAX can supply editable centerlines and junctions and therefore may support annotation, tracing baselines, or quality-control workflows.

main_limitation.text: Its output is parameter-sensitive and may require manual editing, particularly in heterogeneous or anisotropic images.

best_use_case.text: Annotation assistance, classical tracing baseline, and candidate centerline generation rather than automatic ground truth.

transfer_to_sted.rationale: It is microscopy-specific and topology-oriented, but parameter sensitivity and imaging-specific artifacts require validation on the actual STED acquisition.
assumptions: STED intensity ridges correspond sufficiently well to fiber centerlines.
risks: Dense crossings and heterogeneous SNR may require substantial correction.
Using SOAX outputs as labels can propagate method bias.

comparison_summary.task_focus: classical centerline, junction, and topology extraction
comparison_summary.best_use_case: annotation aid and classical tracing baseline

evidence_spans.text: SOAX extracts 3D biopolymer-network centerlines and junctions with Stretching Open Active Contours and provides visualization, editing, and quantitative analysis.
evidence_spans.notes: The introduction explicitly states parameter dependence on biopolymer type and SNR.

evidence_spans.text: SOAX initializes contours on ridges, evolves and stretches them, forms T-junctions, removes overlap, configures junctions, and permits manual contour editing.
evidence_spans.notes: The method operates in 2D or 3D.

evidence_spans.section: Evaluating extraction results and choice of optimal parameters
evidence_spans.text: Synthetic ground truth is evaluated with Hausdorff distance and vertex error; ridge threshold and stretch factor have under- and over-detection regimes, and an F-function is proposed for candidate selection.
evidence_spans.notes: The page gives an example optimum but the card avoids treating it as universal.

evidence_spans.text: The paper demonstrates SOAX on 3D confocal actin-bundle data and uses extracted contours for density and intensity analysis.
evidence_spans.notes: Additional microtubule and yeast examples appear later.

evidence_spans.locator: Discussion of 2D use, wide-field background, anisotropic resolution, and runtime
evidence_spans.text: The authors state that wide-field background may require deconvolution and anisotropic confocal z resolution can create false z-aligned contours; selective initialization and z damping are provided.
evidence_spans.notes: The same page reports order-of-minutes extraction time for shown single frames.

evidence_spans.section: Evaluating extraction results and choice of optimal parameters
evidence_spans.text: Valid F-function parameters can be restricted to a small range, but the workflow still asks the user to choose among candidate optima; sensitivity and guided fine-tuning increase at low SNR.
evidence_spans.notes: The procedure is semi-automatic rather than parameter-free.

bibliography.title: Automated and semi-automated enhancement, segmentation and tracing of cytoskeletal networks in microscopic images: A review

review_notes: A second pass checked methods, figures, tables, results, available appendices or supplements, and limitations against the local PDF.
This card records secondary review synthesis only; Tables 1-3 and the conclusion were checked as review evidence.
Independent human review remains outstanding.

domain.raw_value: review of cytoskeletal-network enhancement, segmentation, and tracing

imaging_modalities.raw_value: multiple microscopy modalities including confocal, STED, SMLM, SIM, TIRF, and electron microscopy

task_levels.raw_value: taxonomy and synthesis of enhancement, segmentation, tracing, and tracking methods

summary.text: The review organizes microscopy constraints and classical, model-based, and deep-learning approaches for cytoskeletal enhancement, segmentation, tracing, and related analysis.

family.raw_value: narrative review rather than a segmentation architecture

details.text: The review distinguishes binary, semantic, instance, supervised, unsupervised, weakly supervised, classical, and deep-learning approaches.

inputs.value: published literature on microscopic cytoskeletal-network image analysis

data.value: cytoskeletal segmentation and tracing studies across classical and deep-learning categories

validation_design.text: This is a narrative field review; cited methods are summarized rather than re-evaluated on a common benchmark.

claimed_contributions.text: The review aims to summarize automated and semi-automated enhancement, segmentation, and tracing methods designed for microscopic cytoskeletal networks.

author_stated_limitations.text: The authors acknowledge that some relevant work could not be covered because of space constraints.

other_reported_findings.text: The review describes annotation difficulty and cost as a major limitation of supervised deep learning for microscopy and expects more weakly, semi-, and unsupervised work.
The review describes weakly supervised U-Net-based segmentation of F-actin nanostructures from STED images and emphasizes that dense intersections remain difficult.
The review states that low SNR, blur, discontinuous contours, crossings, and skeletonization/tracing requirements make cytoskeletal analysis more demanding than simple binary segmentation.

main_strength.text: The review supplies field-level context on microscopy constraints, annotation burden, and the distinction between region masks, centerlines, and instances.

main_limitation.text: Review statements are secondary evidence and the 2021 coverage cannot establish performance of newer methods such as the 2026 ToFiE preprint.

best_use_case.text: Framing corpus gaps, terminology, microscopy constraints, and annotation/evaluation questions.

assumptions: The cited STED constraints remain relevant to this project's acquisition protocol.
risks: Secondary summaries may omit implementation details or study-specific limitations.

domain.raw_value: topology-aware 3D reconstruction of biological fiber networks

imaging_modalities.raw_value: 3D confocal fluorescence microscopy and simulated confocal stacks

task_levels.raw_value: conversion of refined skeleton to an undirected graph

summary.text: ToFiE preprocesses 3D microscopy stacks, extracts a discrete-Morse 1-manifold with DisPerSe, simplifies it with persistent homology, refines fibers and junctions, and converts the result to a NetworkX graph.

family.raw_value: semi-automated discrete Morse theory and persistent-homology workflow

details.text: The three stages are image preprocessing, topology-oriented skeletonization, and skeleton refinement into biologically defined fibers, junctions, and graph connectivity.

outputs.raw_value: undirected NetworkX graph with nodes and fiber edges

data.value: simulated 30-micrometer cubic confocal stacks with 0.1-micrometer voxels and varied photon-count noise
3D confocal fluorescence images of collagen I gels at three concentrations and two polymerization temperatures

postprocessing.value: Gaussian and median filtering, slice-wise intensity normalization, and Richardson-Lucy deconvolution
persistent-homology threshold removes lower-persistence topological features from the DisPerSe skeleton
redefine junction-to-junction fibers, merge or remove short fibers, merge shallow-angle fibers, remove broken or optional dangling ends, and convert to graph
Supplementary Figure S1 reports persistence thresholds 40 (synthetic) and 20 (collagen), and length thresholds 0.65 µm (synthetic) and 0.4 µm (collagen)

value: Kullback-Leibler divergence for edge-length and orientation distributions

metrics.value: junction accuracy from 50 manually inspected junctions per reconstruction by two observers

validation_design.text: Synthetic networks with known topology are rendered as noisy confocal stacks and compared with ground truth; collagen reconstructions are assessed across preparation conditions and with manual junction inspection.

reported_results.text: For the stated synthetic experiments, edge-length KLD remains about 0.1 above SNR 0.75, and junction recall reaches 0.99 for degree 3 and 0.95 for degree 4 before declining below SNR 1.
Recall drops notably for junction connectivity above six, and the authors report that increasing the short-edge threshold can merge nearby junctions and improve this behavior.
Manual inspection of 50 junctions per reconstruction by two observers yields an approximately 0.75 junction-accuracy score across collagen conditions.

claimed_contributions.text: The authors present ToFiE as a semi-automated topology-aware workflow for 3D fiber-network reconstruction from microscopy data.

author_stated_limitations.text: Performance decreases for highly connected synthetic junctions, the workflow requires user-defined parameters, and it does not link reconstructions across time steps.

other_reported_findings.text: The authors contrast persistence thresholding with Otsu thresholding, claiming that under-tracing simplifies while retaining connected topology whereas intensity thresholding can fragment bundles or create skeleton artifacts.

main_strength.text: ToFiE is the corpus's most direct primary source for explicit 3D graph topology recovery from dense microscopy images.

main_limitation.text: It is a parameterized 2026 preprint evaluated on simulated and confocal collagen networks, not STED cytoskeletal data.

best_use_case.text: A topology-aware classical reconstruction baseline and a source of graph-level evaluation ideas for 3D data.

transfer_to_sted.rationale: The workflow targets dense microscopy networks and graph topology, but modality, biological structure, parameters, and preprint status require independent validation.
assumptions: The STED data are 3D or can support meaningful 3D topology extraction.
risks: Persistent features may not correspond to biological fibers under STED artifacts.
Manual parameter tuning may limit throughput and reproducibility.

comparison_summary.task_focus: topology-aware 3D fiber skeleton and graph reconstruction
comparison_summary.main_transfer_risk: parameterized preprint validated on confocal collagen

evidence_spans.text: The preprint introduces a semi-automated topology-aware workflow for reconstructing dense 3D biological fiber networks from high-resolution microscopy images.
evidence_spans.notes: PDF page 1 is a graphical abstract; the manuscript abstract begins on PDF page 2.

evidence_spans.text: The workflow has image preprocessing, topology-preserving skeletonization using DisPerSe, and skeleton refinement into fibers, junctions, and connectivity.
evidence_spans.notes: Printed-page numbering begins after the graphical abstract.

evidence_spans.text: Preprocessing uses Gaussian and median filters, intensity normalization, and Richardson-Lucy deconvolution; DMT and persistent homology extract and simplify a DisPerSe 1-manifold.
evidence_spans.notes: The persistence threshold removes lower-persistence features associated with noise.

evidence_spans.text: Refinement redefines fibers between junctions, handles short and shallow-angle fibers, removes ends, and converts the skeleton to an undirected NetworkX graph.
evidence_spans.notes: The text distinguishes broken-end and optional dangling-end removal.

evidence_spans.text: Synthetic networks are rendered as 30-micrometer cubes with 0.1-micrometer voxels, varied photon counts, and evaluated with KLD and junction recall.
evidence_spans.notes: The simulator models confocal acquisition.

evidence_spans.text: Collagen gels at three concentrations and two temperatures are imaged by confocal fluorescence microscopy; two observers inspect 50 junctions per reconstruction for a junction-accuracy score.
evidence_spans.notes: The experimental object is collagen I.

evidence_spans.text: The paper reports edge-length KLD near 0.1 above SNR 0.75 and recall 0.99 for degree-3 and 0.95 for degree-4 junctions, with degradation below SNR 1.
evidence_spans.notes: Values apply to the stated synthetic setup.

evidence_spans.text: Recall declines above connectivity six; increasing the length threshold can merge nearby junctions, and persistence-threshold behavior is contrasted with Otsu skeletonization.
evidence_spans.notes: The Otsu comparison is an author interpretation.

evidence_spans.text: The workflow uses user-defined parameters and does not include temporal tracking; the authors describe broader modality applications as future potential.
evidence_spans.notes: Claims of broad applicability are not treated as verified STED performance.

evidence_spans.text: Fifty random junctions per reconstruction are manually assessed by two observers, giving a junction-accuracy score of approximately 0.75 across conditions.
evidence_spans.notes: This is experimental collagen validation, not synthetic recall.

evidence_spans.text: Figure S1 reports separate selected parameter values for synthetic and collagen reconstructions, including persistence thresholds 40 and 20 and length thresholds 0.65 µm and 0.4 µm, respectively.
evidence_spans.notes: The parameter differences reinforce that the workflow is dataset- and modality-parameterized.
